prompt.context: We run a manufacturing business in the Southeastern U.S. and have a number of salespeople who are consistently reimbursed for gas. We have 30 salespeople spread throughout the country across 3 regions — East, Central, and West — with 10 per region.
prompt.question: (1) What was the cost of gas last year? (2) How will our expenses be affected going forward? (3) Do you have any recommendations on what we can do to curb our expenses?

clarifying_info.q: How much does a typical salesperson drive?
clarifying_info.a: 1,000 miles per week on average, but there are three driver categories: low (500 mi/wk), medium (1,000 mi/wk), and high (1,500 mi/wk), with 5 low, 15 medium, and 10 high mileage drivers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the vehicle fuel efficiency?
Are salespeople reimbursed for personal use?
clarifying_info.a: They are not supposed to be, but it does happen.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other gasoline uses (delivery trucks, factory machines, etc.)?
clarifying_info.a: There are, but do not worry about them for this case.

clarifying_info.q: What are the plans for the sales force going forward?
clarifying_info.a: No change in habits or mileage is planned for the coming year.

clarifying_info.q: Do all drivers use the same octane level?
clarifying_info.a: Assume everyone uses one octane level of gas.

framework: Define scope: salespeople gas reimbursement only (other uses excluded)
Calculate total miles driven per year by driver category (low/medium/high)
Convert miles to gallons using fuel efficiency (30 mpg)
Apply assumed average gas price (consider breaking into quarters to reflect price variation)
Project forward under best/worst/most-likely gas price scenarios

questions.prompt: Question 1: Calculate the total gasoline cost for the sales force last year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the 30 drivers into three mileage tiers, compute annual miles for each tier, convert to gallons, and multiply by an assumed average gas price. A quarterly breakdown to capture price variation through the year is a differentiating move. Building in a personal-use cushion shows analytical completeness.

math.setup: Driver tiers: 5 low (500 mi/wk), 15 medium (1,000 mi/wk), 10 high (1,500 mi/wk). Weeks/year = 50 (or 52). MPG = 30. Candidate assumes avg gas price (e.g., $3.50/gal or broken into quarterly estimates).
steps: Annual miles by tier (using 50 wks): Low = 5 × 500 × 50 = 125,000 mi; Medium = 15 × 1,000 × 50 = 750,000 mi; High = 10 × 1,500 × 50 = 750,000 mi
math.answer: Approximately $190K–$210K depending on assumed gas price and personal-use cushion.

questions.prompt: Question 2: How will expenses change going forward given rising gas prices?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build three scenarios (best, worst, most likely) around future gas prices, holding mileage constant. Clearly label assumptions for each scenario and show the resulting annual cost. Sensitivity to price changes should be quantified.

math.setup: Total gallons ≈ 54,167/yr (no change in mileage). Vary gas price assumption.
math.answer: Expenses range from ~$135K (best) to ~$271K (worst) depending on gas price scenario, compared to a ~$190K baseline.

questions.prompt: Question 3: What recommendations would you make to curb gasoline expenses?
questions.guidance: Looking for creative, practical, and implementable ideas beyond simple cost-cutting. Strong answers cover control/visibility mechanisms, policy changes, and hedging strategies.

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations can we make to reduce and control the company's gasoline reimbursement expenses?

categories.name: Controls & Policy
ideas: Set per-mile or per-week reimbursement caps
Reimburse only for one standard octane grade
Require mileage logs or GPS-verified trip records
Separate personal vs. business mileage tracking

categories.name: Visibility & Reporting
ideas: Issue company gas cards to capture real-time spending data
Require monthly expense reports with odometer readings
Flag outliers (unusually high reimbursements) for manager review

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Negotiate corporate fuel discount cards (e.g., fleet discount programs)
Route optimization software to reduce miles driven per sales call
Cluster sales territories to minimize travel distances
Allow remote or phone sales where geography permits

categories.name: Financial Hedging
ideas: Purchase oil/gas futures or options to lock in fuel prices
Enter fixed-price fuel contracts with a regional distributor

categories.name: Vehicle & Efficiency
ideas: Incentivize or require higher-MPG personal vehicles for reimbursement eligibility
Consider company-owned high-efficiency fleet vehicles for high-mileage drivers
Explore hybrid or electric vehicle allowances

recommendation: Total gasoline cost last year was approximately $190K–$210K; with rising prices the worst-case forward cost could reach ~$270K, a ~40% increase.
Implement gas cards immediately for full spending visibility and to prevent personal-use leakage.
Introduce tiered reimbursement caps and territory clustering to structurally reduce miles driven.
risks: Gas prices are volatile; a spike beyond worst-case assumptions could exceed budgeted exposure.
Tighter reimbursement controls could cause friction or reduce morale among the sales force.
Hedging strategies require treasury capability and carry their own market risk if prices fall.
next_steps: Issue company gas cards within 30 days to capture baseline spend data.
Conduct territory analysis to identify route-optimization opportunities.
Evaluate feasibility of an oil/gas futures hedge with the CFO.
Review and update reimbursement policy with HR and legal before next fiscal year.
